blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Valuation reps, lesson 6: Price to book and return on equity: the banking and insurance lens.

Royal Bank trades today at roughly two point one times book value. TD trades closer to one point six. Same country, same regulator, same deposit insurance regime. The gap is not noise, it is return on equity speaking through the price.

Here is why price to book matters specifically for banks and insurers, and why you'd never lean on it for a software company. A bank's balance sheet is mostly financial assets and liabilities marked close to fair value. Loans, securities, deposits. Book value for a bank is a real economic number, not an accounting fiction full of goodwill and depreciated factories. So price to book becomes a clean read on what the market thinks the bank earns on that book, which is return on equity.

The mechanical link: price to book roughly equals return on equity divided by cost of equity, adjusted for growth. Royal Bank posted return on equity near sixteen percent in its most recent fiscal year, fiscal 2024 ending October. TD's return on equity has been dragged down by the US anti-money-laundering penalties and asset cap, sitting closer to eleven or twelve percent. Higher return on equity, higher price to book, every time, across the sector. You can pull both numbers in Thomson ONE under the ratios tab, return on equity and price to book sit side by side, no calculation needed.

The mistake people make is comparing price to book across sectors, or worse, assuming a low price to book bank is cheap. A bank trading below one times book usually means the market expects return on equity to stay below cost of equity, or it's pricing in credit losses not yet on the balance sheet. That's not value, that's a warning the market already read.

What this multiple reveals: relative profitability within a homogeneous balance sheet sector, fast and clean. What it cannot tell you: capital adequacy, loan book quality, or where we are in the credit cycle. It's a lens, not a verdict. You still need the analysis underneath before you let a ratio argue your case.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 23: Disability insurance: own occupation, elimination period, and the taxable versus non-taxable choice.

Here's the mistake that costs clients six figures. They buy disability insurance on price, and they don't read the definition of disability. For a professional, that one clause decides whether the policy actually pays when it matters.

Own occupation means the insurer pays a benefit if you can't perform the specific duties of your own job, even if you go work at something else. For a surgeon who develops a hand tremor, own occupation means she gets paid even if she retrains as a medical consultant earning good money elsewhere. A weaker "any occupation" definition means she gets nothing once she's capable of any job, full stop. For incorporated professionals, own occupation is close to non-negotiable. It costs more, usually fifteen to twenty-five percent more in premium, but it's the entire point of the purchase.

Elimination period is the waiting time between disability onset and when benefits start, commonly 90 days, sometimes 120 or 180. Longer elimination periods lower your premium but mean you're funding your own overhead and living costs out of savings or a line of credit for that stretch. For a business owner with an overhead expense policy running alongside, matching the two elimination periods matters, because a mismatch creates a gap month where nothing pays.

Now the taxable versus non-taxable choice, and this is the one people get backwards. If the corporation pays the premium as a deductible expense, the eventual benefit is taxable income to you. If you pay the premium personally with after-tax dollars, the benefit comes out tax-free. Worked example: a benefit of 8,000 dollars a month. Taxed at a marginal rate of 43 percent in Manitoba for 2025, that corporate-paid policy nets you roughly 4,560 dollars a month when you need it most. The personally-paid policy nets the full 8,000. The premium saving from having the corporation pay is almost never worth the tax hit during a claim.

The single mistake: business owners let the corporation pay the premium to save a few hundred dollars a year in cash flow, without running the net-benefit math.

Communication, lesson 23: Written communication: emails that get read and get a reply.

Todd Rogers at Harvard's Kennedy School studied thousands of real emails and found something uncomfortable: the single biggest predictor of whether someone replies isn't the subject line or the tone. It's length. Rogers and his colleagues showed that emails under 75 to 100 words get replies at dramatically higher rates than longer ones, and the drop-off starts fast after that.

Here's the mechanism. Your client reads your email on a phone, between two other tasks, with maybe eight seconds of attention. If the ask isn't visible without scrolling, you've lost the moment. The email isn't ignored out of disrespect. It's deferred, and deferred usually means dead.

Worked example. Bad version: four paragraphs explaining market context, a recap of your last call, then buried in paragraph three, "let me know if you'd like to revisit your bond allocation." Good version: "Given rates moved 0.5 percent this quarter, I think we should shift 10 percent of your bond sleeve into shorter duration. Fifteen minutes Thursday or Friday to confirm?" That's 34 words. One decision, one number, one time-bound ask.

The one mistake: putting the ask at the end instead of the top. People write like they're building a case, lawyer-style, saving the verdict for last. Readers don't owe you that patience. Lead with the decision you want, then justify it in one line if needed.

For your practice task today, pull the last three emails you sent to clients. Find the actual ask in each one, and check where it sits. If it's not in the first sentence, you've found your pattern.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Apotex, Cohere and Xanadu Lead Business News
blocks.script:
Apotex is in the news first. It is Canada's largest generic drugmaker, now public after its own initial public offering, and the Globe profiles chief executive Jeff Watson launching a generic GLP-one weight loss drug. The tailwind is massive global demand for cheaper GLP-ones. The headwind is patent fights with Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly. An evidence-based advisor says own the sector through a fund, do not chase one newly public name.

Cohere is next. The Toronto AI company caught a rival model, Alibaba's Qwen, trying to upload a file to a server in Beijing, the Globe reports. The tailwind is credibility as the security-conscious Canadian AI vendor. The headwind is that the episode feeds broader fear about unpredictable model behaviour. Cohere is private, so an advisor tells you there are no shares to buy, only policy to watch.

Alibaba, the Chinese e-commerce and cloud giant, is the other side of that story. The tailwind is Qwen's global reach, proof its AI ambitions are scaling fast. The headwind is this incident deepens Western distrust of Chinese AI touching sensitive systems. An advisor says Chinese tech carries real regulatory and geopolitical risk, so size any position small.

OMERS, the Ontario municipal pension giant, trimmed its stake in quantum computing firm Xanadu and recouped its original cost, the Globe reports. The tailwind is vindication for an early venture bet made before quantum hype peaked. The headwind is quantum computing still generates no meaningful revenue. An advisor notes pension funds take illiquid venture risk you cannot replicate in a normal portfolio.

Xanadu itself, a Toronto quantum computing startup racing to build a commercially useful machine, benefits from having OMERS as a validated backer for future funding rounds. The headwind is a commercial product remains years off. An advisor says this is venture-stage risk, unsuitable for most retail accounts.

blocks.title: Wealthsimple's $13.8-Billion Round Reshapes the Competitive Map
blocks.script:
Wealthsimple just raised up to four hundred twenty five million dollars at a thirteen point eight billion dollar valuation, up thirty eight percent from ten billion a year ago. GIC led the round, with Power Corporation and IGM Financial topping up to protect their stake. Assets under administration hit one hundred sixty nine point two billion dollars, and the firm is openly chasing a trillion, which would put it on par with the big banks. For you, the signal is pricing and service pressure. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada found clients pay fifty to one hundred fifty dollars per registered account just to transfer out of a bank, a friction fee that firms like Wealthsimple don't charge. If a client mentions switching, know that number cold.

Worth noting, Wealthsimple's own CEO flagged that Canada's new prediction market guidance from CIRO and the provincial regulators leaves key questions unresolved as the firm pushes into that space. Watch for follow up bulletins if you have clients curious about event contracts.

Closer to home, the Manitoba Securities Commission has formally transferred registration duties for investment dealers and mutual fund dealer firms to CIRO, tidying up a gap that lagged other provinces. If you're dealing with MSC on a registration file, route it to CIRO now.

Separately, an IG Wealth study finds most advisors want to grow their affluent client base but say their own dealer firms aren't equipped to help them do it, worth raising if you're weighing a move to an independent.

Three quick notes from elsewhere in today's briefing. If the Bank of Canada does hike, flag variable rate and line of credit clients today, not next week. The housing correction being mostly an Ontario and B.C. story means Manitoba clients weighing a move east need updated comparables, not national headlines. And with RBC blocking AI agents from its banking login, remind every client: never hand banking credentials to an AI tool, full stop.
talkingPoints: Wealthsimple's valuation jump shows where fee pressure is heading, know your transfer-out costs.
Manitoba registration files now route through CIRO, not the MSC directly.
Prediction market rules are still unsettled, pause before recommending event contracts.
A rate hike today means a same-day call to variable rate and credit line clients.
Never let a client type banking passwords into an AI assistant.

blocks.title: Election Day, ER Doctors Push Back, Extradition Case
blocks.script:
Manitobans are voting right now in the municipal election, and this is the one that matters most to anything you do with civic files or infrastructure clients. Polls close at eight tonight in Winnipeg's mayoral race, with twelve candidates on the ballot, fifty-four running for council, and more than ninety for school trustee. Advance turnout gave a hint of the mood: the Free Press reports advance polls saw a record 50,767 Winnipeggers vote, up 21 per cent from the previous high set in 2022. Mayor Scott Gillingham has campaigned on a costed platform that includes a property tax hike, while Mayor's race outsider Noah Redden picked up a notable endorsement from former mayor Glen Murray. Results roll in tonight, so expect this to dominate client conversation tomorrow regardless of outcome.

On health policy, two stories for your files. A Manitoba man with a degenerative disease will keep access to his drug after the province stepped in with coverage, following a federal funding reversal, CBC reports. And more pointedly for the health system: over 60 emergency doctors in Winnipeg sent a letter asking the province to pause discussions on a virtual care initiative for emergency rooms. Physicians at Health Sciences Centre and St. Boniface Hospital say they only learned of the proposal days before vendor site visits, and health minister Uzoma Asagwara says the province is still in a consultation phase with no decisions made.

Two items worth flagging on compliance and reputational risk. Canada's privacy commissioner is opening an investigation into the Crime Stoppers data breach, focused on Navigate 360, the U.S. third party that managed the tip line's data. And a Winnipeg man, Ajay Singh, is fighting extradition to the United States over allegations he used fake payroll numbers to secure more than 11.5 million U.S. dollars in pandemic relief loans, with over 600,000 dollars still unaccounted for, CBC reports.

On a lighter note, three Blue Bombers, Brady Oliveira, Jarell Broxton, and Major Williams, are finalists for the CFL's top Canadian award, a nice talking point if clients are Bombers season ticket holders heading into the playoffs.

blocks.title: Canada's new ties with the EU will be closer to membership than anything done before, officials say
blocks.script:
Bigger picture, Canada and the European Union meet this week in Montreal for a summit aimed at a new associate membership arrangement. blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Free cash flow: three definitions and which one to use / Physician specific planning: overhead, disability coverage, and income smoothing / Storytelling with clients: the three stories every advisor should have ready
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Statement forensics, lesson 5: Free cash flow: three definitions and which one to use.

Three analysts can look at the same company and hand you three different free cash flow numbers, and none of them are wrong. That's the problem. Free cash flow isn't on the financial statements, it's built, and the way it's built changes the story.

Definition one: operating cash flow minus capital expenditure. This is the simplest and the most common, and it's what you'll find pre-calculated on Thomson ONE under the cash flow summary tab. Definition two: operating cash flow minus maintenance capex only, leaving growth spending untouched. This tells you what the business throws off if it stopped expanding. Definition three, the one equity analysts lean on for valuation: net income plus depreciation and amortization, minus capex, minus the change in working capital. This one reconciles back to the income statement, which matters when you're arguing with someone who distrusts cash flow statements generally.

Take a real example. Costco, fiscal year 2024. Operating cash flow was about 11.3 billion dollars. Total capital expenditure was about 4.6 billion. Simple free cash flow: 6.7 billion. Now, Costco's growth capex, mostly new warehouses, was roughly 60 percent of that spend. Strip that out for maintenance-only, and free cash flow jumps to something closer to 9 billion. Same company, same year, a 2.3 billion dollar swing depending on which definition you picked.

The mistake people make is citing "free cash flow" as if it's a single audited figure, the way they'd cite revenue. It isn't audited. It's a calculation, and the capex split inside it is often a guess, not a disclosed line. When someone hands you a free cash flow number without naming which formula they used, you don't have information, you have an opinion wearing a number's clothes.

The evidence-based view: free cash flow tells you cash generation after reinvestment, which net income alone cannot. It cannot tell you, on its own, whether that reinvestment was necessary or discretionary. That split is tomorrow's lesson.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 22: Physician specific planning: overhead, disability coverage, and income smoothing.

Here's the number that surprises most physicians when you say it out loud: overhead runs 30 to 40 percent of gross billings for a typical family medicine or specialist office in Manitoba, before the doctor takes home a dollar. Staff, rent, equipment leases, billing software, malpractice coverage through the Canadian Medical Protective Association. That overhead doesn't stop if the doctor gets sick. It keeps billing the corporation every month whether the physician is in the office or in a hospital bed.

This is why overhead expense insurance is a separate product from personal disability insurance, and why physicians need both. Personal disability replaces the physician's own income. Overhead expense insurance replaces the fixed costs of running the practice during a disability, typically for 12 to 24 months, so the clinic doesn't fold while the doctor recovers.

Here's a worked example. A solo-practice physician in Winnipeg bills 450,000 dollars a year through her medical professional corporation. Overhead, including two staff salaries, rent, and equipment, is 150,000 dollars a year, about 12,500 a month. She takes personal disability coverage for her own income replacement, say 10,000 a month, but she has no overhead expense policy. She has a stroke in February 2026. For six months she can't work. Personal disability pays her, but the 75,000 dollars in overhead that accrued over those six months comes straight out of corporate retained earnings, the same retained earnings she'd been using for an individual pension plan contribution strategy from lesson 20. The IPP funding gets deferred a year.

The one mistake: physicians buy personal disability and assume it covers the practice too. It doesn't. The policies are priced and underwritten completely separately, and overhead expense premiums are generally tax deductible to the corporation as a business expense, unlike personal disability premiums, which are not deductible when paid personally.

Communication, lesson 22: Storytelling with clients: the three stories every advisor should have ready.

Annette Simmons, author of "The Story Factor," argues that facts persuade for about ten seconds and stories persuade for the length of the relationship. You already know your pacing and your eye line. Now you need the actual material to say.

Every advisor sitting across from a client, or on a board, or recording a LinkedIn video, needs exactly three stories ready, not twenty.

Story one: the origin story. Why you do this work. Not "I got into finance after college." Something specific. One advisor I worked with tells clients his father retired with enough money but no plan for his time, and died eighteen months later of what the family quietly called boredom. That's the reason he builds retirement plans around purpose, not just numbers. Takes forty seconds to tell.

Story two: the turnaround story. A client who was heading toward a bad outcome and you changed the trajectory. Real numbers matter here. Not "I helped someone save more." Say: a client was on pace to run out of money at age 81 based on a 4% withdrawal rate against a $1.2 million portfolio. You restructured the allocation and delayed Social Security claiming by three years, and the new projection carries him to 94. That specificity is what separates a case study from a brag.

Story three: the failure story. Something you got wrong and what it taught you. This is the one people skip, and it's the one that builds the most trust, per research from Harvard Business School on vulnerability and perceived competence. Clients don't believe perfect people. They believe people who've been burned and adjusted.

The one mistake: using the same story for every audience. The origin story works on camera. The turnaround story works in a sales meeting. The failure story works on a nonprofit board where you're positioning yourself as a peer, not a vendor. Mismatch them and they fall flat.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pull one company's cash flow statement on Thomson ONE and calculate simple free cash flow, operating cash flow minus total capex, for the last two fiscal years, and note the direction of change.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull one physician client's current disability coverage summary and check whether they hold a standalone overhead expense policy, not just personal disability, and note the monthly benefit amount versus their actual fixed overhead.
Communication: Write out your turnaround story in six sentences, with one real number in it, and time yourself saying it out loud. It should land between 40 and 60 seconds.

blocks.script:
Start with the Federal Court of Appeal. On September 2nd, the court sided with the Canada Revenue Agency in a long-running fight with accounting firm Zeifmans LLP, as the Globe and Mail's Advisor Daily reports today. The case goes back to 2019, when the CRA demanded five years of records tied to three named clients plus unnamed entities connected to them. A lower court had blocked the order, saying the CRA needed prior judicial authorization for anything touching unnamed parties. The Court of Appeal reversed that. The test now: if the unnamed-person information is sought to verify a named client already under audit, CRA does not need court approval first. If you have incorporated business owner or physician clients with related corporations, trusts, or holding companies, this matters. A requirement letter naming your client can sweep in connected entities without a separate court step. If clients mention this, treat it like the Capital One breach settlement Investment Executive covered today, where a thirty-five million dollar deal is delivering roughly twenty-four and a half million to six million affected Canadians. blocks.script:
Winnipeggers vote today for mayor, council and school trustees, and the race has tightened down the stretch. A new poll has given mayoral candidate Shaun Loney's rival Kevin Klein a boost, with the Free Press reporting that gives Redden momentum, while incumbent Scott Gillingham still leads among decided voters even though nearly 60 per cent of respondents told pollsters someone else should be running the city. Gillingham has put numbers to his platform, promising a 3.5 per cent property tax increase in 2027 with no hard cap going forward, which Klein has seized on, questioning why anyone would trust a repeat of past promises. If you've got clients with downtown commercial holdings or rental portfolios, today's result shapes the tax and development file for the next four years.

The bigger structural story for your Churchill-exposed clients: Dubai's DP World has signed a memorandum of understanding with Arctic Gateway Group and CentrePort to help build out trade through the Port of Churchill, linking Manitoba to DP World's global network of more than sixty ports. The federal transport minister is framing it as part of Canada's push for new export corridors. But it's not uncontested. Indigenous voices, including campaigners quoted this week, argue there's real community concern about the environmental and social impact of a bigger port, pushing back against claims that opposition doesn't exist. Worth flagging: this comes right after Premier Kinew told Carney and assembled chiefs it's time to abolish the Indian Act, a moment Kinew pushed directly in that closed-door meeting with the Assembly of First Nations.

blocks.script:
Clocks fall back November first here in Manitoba, and paediatric sleep guidance says don't wait until Sunday to deal with it. HealthyChildren.org, the American Academy of Pediatrics' consumer site, recommends starting about a week early: nudge naps and bedtime a few minutes earlier each day, keep dinner earlier too since eating close to bedtime disrupts sleep. Most children adjust within three to seven days, so expect some crankiness, not a crisis.

Separately, the Globe and Mail has a useful distinction for parents right now with Halloween approaching: ordinary fear, like being scared of a costume or the dark, is normal childhood development. Persistent anxiety that interferes with daily life is different and worth raising with a paediatrician. Worth knowing if clients ask about screening or waitlists for child mental health support here in Manitoba.

blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: GDP: nominal, real, per capita, and why Canada's per capita number has been the story / Medical professional corporations: Manitoba rules and share structures / On camera: eye line, energy, and the first five seconds
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Macro & rates, lesson 5: GDP: nominal, real, per capita, and why Canada's per capita number has been the story.

Statistics Canada reported real gross domestic product per capita has fallen or stayed flat in most quarters since early 2023, even while headline GDP kept growing. That gap is the whole story, and almost nobody outside the Bank of Canada's own research notes talks about it properly.

Start with the three numbers. Nominal GDP is the total dollar value of everything produced in the country, measured in today's dollars, no adjustment for inflation. Real GDP strips out inflation so you can compare one year to another on an apples to apples basis. Per capita GDP takes real GDP and divides it by population. That third number tells you whether the average person is actually getting richer, or whether the country is just adding more people.

Here is the worked example. Canada's real GDP grew by roughly 1.1 percent in 2023. Sounds fine on its own. But population grew by about 3.1 percent that same year, the fastest pace since the 1950s, driven mostly by immigration and non permanent residents. Divide it out: real GDP per capita actually fell by close to 2 percent. The economy got bigger. Canadians, on average, got poorer in output terms. On Thomson ONE, you'll find this under the StatsCan GDP release feed, cross reference the population series from the same agency to build the per capita line yourself, because most screens show you headline real GDP and stop there.

The mistake people make is reading quarterly headline GDP growth as "the economy is doing well" without asking what population did underneath it. A country can post positive growth every quarter and still have every resident worse off. That is not a trick of the data, it is the data working exactly as designed, you just have to ask the second question.

What this reveals: whether output is expanding faster than the population consuming it. What it cannot tell you: distribution, who captured the gains, or productivity by sector. For that you still need the analysis layer first, before any chart.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 21: Medical professional corporations: Manitoba rules and share structures.

In Manitoba, under The Medical Act and the College of Physicians and Surgeons rules, a professional corporation can only issue voting shares to the physician who's practising, or to another licensed physician. That's different from provinces like Ontario, where family members can hold non-voting shares directly. In Manitoba, non-voting, non-participating shares can go to the physician's spouse, children, or a family trust, but only as a class separate from the voting class, and the physician must retain all voting control, full stop. There's no shared voting ever.

Here's the worked example. Dr. Patel incorporates in Winnipeg. She holds 100 voting common shares. Her corporation also issues 1,000 non-voting, discretionary dividend shares, held by a family trust with her spouse and two adult children as beneficiaries. In 2026, the corporation earns 400,000 dollars in professional income, pays itself down after overhead, and has 180,000 dollars left to distribute as dividends. Because the non-voting shares carry dividend rights, the corporation can sprinkle dividends to the spouse and kids, each potentially using their own basic personal amount, about 15,705 dollars federally for 2025, plus Manitoba's basic personal amount of 15,969 for 2025, pulling income out at low marginal rates instead of all landing on Dr. Patel personally.

The one mistake people make: assuming the Tax on Split Income rules, called TOSI, don't apply just because it's a professional corporation with family shareholders. TOSI, in effect since 2018, taxes most dividends to adult family members at the top marginal rate unless an exclusion applies, and the main exclusion here is that the family member works in the business at least an average of 20 hours a week during the year, or did so in any five prior years. A spouse who does genuine bookkeeping or admin for the clinic can qualify. One who does nothing doesn't.

Communication, lesson 21: On camera: eye line, energy, and the first five seconds.

Researchers at Stanford, Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass, found people treat screens the way they treat other people: judgments about trust form in seconds, not minutes. Julian Treasure, who studies vocal and visual presence, puts the usable window for camera content at about five seconds before a viewer decides whether to keep watching. That decision is made before you've said anything useful. It's made on eye line and energy.

Eye line first. Your eyes need to hit the lens, not the preview window of your own face. Most laptop setups put the camera above or below eye level, so you end up looking down or up, which reads as either submissive or lecturing. Raise or lower the camera until the lens sits exactly where your eyes naturally land when talking to a peer, roughly the top third of your face in frame.

Energy second. On camera, your natural conversational energy reads as flat, because the camera strips out a third of your expressiveness, something broadcast coaches like Nick Morgan have documented for years. So you need to run about 20 percent hotter than feels natural: more eyebrow movement, more vocal variation, a slightly bigger smile than you think necessary.

Here's the worked example. A financial advisor posts a 90 second LinkedIn video. In the first five seconds he says "Hi, I'm going to talk today about sequence of returns risk." Flat eyes, flat voice, looking slightly below the lens. Average watch time: 11 seconds, per his own analytics. He re-shoots, same script, but opens with "Your retirement plan can go bankrupt in year three and still look fine on paper," eyes locked on the lens, eyebrows up, leaning in. Watch time: 58 seconds.

The mistake: scripting the first five seconds as an introduction instead of a hook, and rehearsing content instead of rehearsing the opening line specifically.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pull Canada's real GDP growth and population growth for the last four quarters from StatsCan or Thomson ONE, and calculate per capita growth for each quarter by hand.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull your Manitoba-incorporated medical client's share structure and confirm in writing which shareholders are voting versus non-voting, and whether any dividend recipient meets the TOSI 20-hour exclusion with documented hours.
Communication: Record three versions of your next video's opening five seconds, same content, varying only eye line and energy, then watch them back muted to judge energy alone.

lessons.label: Communication
lessons.title: On camera: eye line, energy, and the first five seconds
lessons.script:
Researchers at Stanford, Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass, found people treat screens the way they treat other people: judgments about trust form in seconds, not minutes. Julian Treasure, who studies vocal and visual presence, puts the usable window for camera content at about five seconds before a viewer decides whether to keep watching. That decision is made before you've said anything useful. It's made on eye line and energy.

Eye line first. Your eyes need to hit the lens, not the preview window of your own face. Most laptop setups put the camera above or below eye level, so you end up looking down or up, which reads as either submissive or lecturing. Raise or lower the camera until the lens sits exactly where your eyes naturally land when talking to a peer, roughly the top third of your face in frame.

Energy second. On camera, your natural conversational energy reads as flat, because the camera strips out a third of your expressiveness, something broadcast coaches like Nick Morgan have documented for years. So you need to run about 20 percent hotter than feels natural: more eyebrow movement, more vocal variation, a slightly bigger smile than you think necessary.

Here's the worked example. A financial advisor posts a 90 second LinkedIn video. In the first five seconds he says "Hi, I'm going to talk today about sequence of returns risk." Flat eyes, flat voice, looking slightly below the lens. Average watch time: 11 seconds, per his own analytics. He re-shoots, same script, but opens with "Your retirement plan can go bankrupt in year three and still look fine on paper," eyes locked on the lens, eyebrows up, leaning in. Watch time: 58 seconds.

The mistake: scripting the first five seconds as an introduction instead of a hook, and rehearsing content instead of rehearsing the opening line specifically.
lessons.task: Record three versions of your next video's opening five seconds, same content, varying only eye line and energy, then watch them back muted to judge energy alone.
lessons.drill: Film 10 seconds of yourself delivering any opening line. Score two items: eyes on lens for at least 80 percent of the clip (yes or no), and at least two visible energy shifts, eyebrow, lean, or hand gesture (count them). Passing score: yes plus two or more.

blocks.title: Meta, EQT, and a Made-in-Canada Missile Lead
blocks.script:
Start with Meta. The Facebook and Instagram parent, now building out artificial intelligence infrastructure at enormous scale. The Globe reports Meta launched public offerings of about $35 billion in common stock and convertible preferred stock to finance its AI expansion, plus a separate share sale program of up to $60 billion once non-voting Class C shares begin trading. The tailwind: Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have floated interest in buying up to five billion dollars of the shares. The headwind: free cash flow just turned negative. An evidence-based advisor tells a client this is a single stock bet on an unproven AI payoff, not a reason to abandon a diversified portfolio.

Next, EQT and Range Resources together. EQT is a Pennsylvania gas producer, Range Resources an Appalachian driller, and Monday they agreed to merge. The Globe reports the all-stock deal is valued at more than US$50-billion, including debt, creating what the companies called the largest vertically integrated natural gas producer in the United States. The tailwind is data centre power demand. The headwind: Range investors get a fixed exchange ratio, so EQT shares fell over four per cent on the news while Range jumped ten. An advisor would say sector consolidation plays like this belong in a broad energy allocation, not a single-name wager.

Then there is North Vector Dynamics, a Canadian defence startup building low-cost counterdrone missiles. The Globe reports the company raised twenty-nine million dollars to expand manufacturing of its CM-70 precision-guided missile. The tailwind is clear: global demand for cheap drone defence is surging after years of underinvestment. The headwind is execution risk, this is early-stage hardware manufacturing with thin margins until volume arrives. An advisor would flag this as a venture-stage story, fine for risk capital, not core holdings.

Finally, Puppy Sphere. It is a Canadian pet-care startup the Globe profiles today, growing fast after early stumbles. The story is about founders with startup instincts pivoting their model to scale. The tailwind is a loyal customer base and quick adaptation. The headwind is the same one every small growth company faces, funding the next stage without diluting control. An advisor would say private growth stories like this are interesting reading, not something a retail client can easily access or price.

In a September 2 judgment, the court reaffirmed the CRA's broad power to demand client information from third parties like accountants, even when the request touches unnamed people connected to a client. blocks.title: Winnipeg Votes Wednesday, Brandon ER Warnings Escalate
blocks.script:
The biggest story for you this week is Wednesday's vote. Manitoba's municipal elections, including Winnipeg's mayoral race, land on October 28th, and the race has tightened. A new Abacus Data poll done for the Winnipeg Free Press, fielded between October 16th and 22nd, has incumbent Scott Gillingham at 36 per cent among decided voters. That's down 19 percentage points from the same poll in late August and early September. Abacus vice-president Curtis Brown still called it "Scott Gillingham's race to lose," but the margin has closed meaningfully, and twelve candidates are on the ballot. If you've got clients or board colleagues watching city hall, infill zoning, water rates, and densification are the flashpoints challengers Kevin Klein and Michael Vogiatzakis have been pushing. Worth watching Wednesday night for anyone with exposure to city contracts, development permits, or property tax planning.

In Brandon, the Manitoba Nurses Union is warning that chronic staffing shortages at the emergency room are creating escalating safety risks, with mounting security concerns alongside long wait times for patients. That's a rural healthcare story, but it feeds directly into the provincial health funding conversation Manitoba's government will face heading into any spring budget planning.

Separately, a Manitoba man with a rare genetic condition, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, has been denied out-of-province coverage for a procedure he and medical experts say isn't available here. He told CBC he's being "tortured every single day" and is now considering medically assisted dying. It's a stark illustration of the gaps in interprovincial health coverage that Manitoba residents are navigating right now.

One item from British Columbia worth a passing mention for anyone with west coast holdings: incoming premier Lorne Doerkson has pledged to prioritize the province's finances and push a west coast pipeline, which matters if you've got energy exposure tied to export capacity.

Closer to home, Point Douglas residents are pushing the city for crosswalk safety changes after a fatal collision at Main and Jarvis this week, a reminder that infrastructure spending debates in this civic election aren't abstract.

blocks.script: The Globe and Mail asks today whether it's normal for kids to be afraid, timely with Halloween a few days out. The short answer from paediatric bodies: yes, mostly. The Canadian Paediatric Society notes occasional, short-lived fears and worries are a normal part of development, things like separation anxiety, fear of the dark, or fear of strangers. What's different is an anxiety disorder: persistent, disproportionate responses that start interfering with daily functioning, school, friendships, sleep. The Canadian Paediatric Society says that line matters for parents deciding whether to just ride out a scary season or book a pediatrician visit. For clients with young kids or grandkids, this is useful dinner-table context before Halloween decorations and costume parties start triggering genuine fear in toddlers versus the fun kind. Watch for avoidance of normal activities, not just a jump at a mask.

Company & Economy Analysis, Evidence arsenal, lesson 6: Dividend investing: what the evidence supports and what it costs.

Here's the claim you'll hear from a certain kind of advisor: dividend stocks beat the market with less risk, and the dividend itself is the proof of quality. Part of that holds up. Part of it is an accounting illusion.

Start with what the evidence actually supports. Fama and French, and later work using the CRSP database, show that high dividend yield has historically overlapped with value and quality factors. Companies that pay consistent dividends tend to have stable cash flows, lower leverage, and management discipline around capital allocation. That's real. Dividend aristocrats, the S&P 500 names with 25 plus consecutive years of dividend increases, have shown lower volatility than the broad index over multi-decade windows. Standard deviation, not return, is where the case is strongest.

Now the mechanics people get wrong. A dividend is not found money. When a company pays a dollar per share, the share price drops by roughly that dollar on the ex-dividend date. You're not earning extra return, you're converting unrealized capital gain into a cash distribution, often a taxable one. In Thomson ONE, pull up the price chart around any ex-dividend date and you'll see the gap directly, it's not hidden.

Worked example. Take a stock at 50 dollars paying a 2 dollar annual dividend, a 4 percent yield. Total return investor and dividend investor end up in the same place pretax. But the dividend investor now owes tax on that 2 dollars in the 2026 tax year, at rates up to 29 percent federally in Canada above 253,414 dollars of income, while the total return investor who sold shares instead gets the 50 percent capital gains inclusion rate. Same economic outcome, different tax bill.

The one mistake: chasing yield. A 9 percent yield usually means the market has already priced in a dividend cut, not that you found a bargain. Check the payout ratio against free cash flow, not against earnings, before you believe the number.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 20: Corporate owned life insurance: the CDA credit and the planning use.

When a corporation receives a life insurance death benefit, that money doesn't just show up as taxable income. Most of it lands in something called the capital dividend account, the CDA. That account lets the corporation pay money out to shareholders completely tax free, as a capital dividend.

Here's the mechanic for 2026. The amount credited to the CDA equals the death benefit received, minus the adjusted cost basis of the policy at the time of death. The adjusted cost basis is roughly the sum of premiums paid, less the pure insurance cost over the years, with some adjustments for dividends and loans. For most permanent policies held a long time, the adjusted cost basis shrinks toward zero, so almost the entire death benefit ends up in the CDA.

Worked example. Say a corporation owns a two million dollar permanent policy on its owner. At death, the adjusted cost basis is sixty thousand dollars. The CDA credit is one million nine hundred forty thousand dollars. That amount can go to the estate, through the shareholder's estate holding the shares, as a tax free capital dividend. The remaining sixty thousand flows through as a taxable dividend, which still gets preferential treatment but isn't free.

The planning use is clear: this is one of the only ways to move large sums out of a corporation to an estate with zero personal tax, which matters enormously for incorporated business owners and medical professionals who've built up value inside the corp and want a clean, tax efficient transfer at death.

The one mistake people make is assuming the full death benefit is tax free without checking the adjusted cost basis calculation, or forgetting that filing the capital dividend election, form T2054, has to happen before the dividend is paid. Miss that election or get it wrong, and the Canada Revenue Agency can treat the whole dividend as taxable. There's also a trap when corporate-owned policies are transferred between corporations or shareholders, since that can trigger a disposition and change the adjusted cost basis math entirely.

Communication, lesson 20: Vocal delivery: pace, pitch, and the monotone trap on camera.

Julian Treasure, who has given some of the most watched TED talks on sound and listening, built his whole framework on one finding: humans decide whether to trust a voice within seconds, based on pitch variation and pace, before they even process the words. He calls a flat, unvarying voice "monotone" and says it signals boredom or deception to the listener's ear, even when the speaker means neither.

Here is the mechanism. Average conversational speech runs about 150 words per minute. On camera, nerves push most people to 170 or 180 without noticing. At that speed, with pitch staying inside a narrow band, maybe 20 hertz of range instead of the 60 to 80 hertz a natural storyteller uses, the voice reads as a drone. Your advisor clients already associate that drone with scripted, low-trust content, the kind they scroll past.

Try the math on a 90 second LinkedIn video. At 150 words per minute, that is 225 words. Most people script 280 to 300 words for that same slot because they're writing for reading speed, not speaking speed, then they rush to fit it in. The rushing flattens pitch because there's no time to breathe between phrases, and breath is where pitch variation lives.

The one mistake: people fix pace but not pitch. They slow down and still sound flat, because slowing down alone doesn't restore the up and down movement that signals sincerity. You need both, and pitch is the one nobody rehearses.

blocks.title: Stelco, Cymax, Banks Lead Business Headlines
blocks.script:
Stelco, the Hamilton steelmaker now owned by Cleveland-Cliffs, is this week's test case for Ottawa, with the Globe's own quiz asking how long it has to respond to government demands. Tailwind: federal leverage that could protect jobs. Headwind: compliance and legal risk. An evidence-based advisor says single-company political bets are speculation, not investing.

blocks.title: Succession Gaps, CRA Rates, and Cyber Trust Risk
blocks.script:
A US jury has ordered Meta to pay twenty five billion dollars hours before its earnings print, tied to forty three million violations around misleading consumers, per Wealth Professional. Meta plans to appeal, but if you hold big tech concentration in client portfolios, this is a reminder to stress test single stock exposure against headline risk, not just earnings risk.

Closer to home, the Canada Revenue Agency has held the prescribed interest rate at three percent for a seventh straight quarter, Advisor.ca reports. That keeps income splitting loans to a spouse or a family trust affordable, but watch the alternative minimum tax interaction before you set up a new loan, especially for incorporated professionals using a holding company structure.

The bigger story for your incorporated business owner clients: a new CFIB report finds most Canadian owners have no formal exit plan, putting two trillion dollars in business value at risk, per Wealth Professional. If you have a physician or any professional corporation client past fifty five, this is your opening to book a succession conversation now, before a health event or a buyer forces the timeline.

Pair that with new Wells Fargo research showing inheritance conflict is the norm, not the exception, among wealthy families. For blended families or clients mid divorce, that is the moment to push a family meeting before assets move, not after.

On cybersecurity, the global PHP flaw has advisors across Canada facing real client trust questions, Wealth Professional reports. If you have not confirmed your dealer's breach notification protocol this month, do it before a client asks you first.

Kevin Klein is pushing a question about a bylaw contract, a zoning rewrite deal awarded to an American company, and Scott Gillingham says that one is now with the city auditor to review. blocks.title: Joly demands Stelco owner comply with job commitments in new letter, gives 15-day deadline to respond
blocks.script:
Ottawa has given Cleveland-Cliffs fifteen days to reverse layoffs at Stelco or face court action. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly sent a demand letter to the Ohio-based owner, saying the company is violating its commitments under the Investment Canada Act and it has 15 days to resolve the issue. The dispute traces back to Cliffs chief executive Lourenco Goncalves, who backed Trump's tariffs before cutting jobs in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ontario. Commentary in the Globe disputes the company's steel-dumping justification, calling the position contradictory given the CEO's earlier tariff advocacy.

Prime Minister Carney was in Ankara today, where he and Turkish President Erdoğan unveiled a three-year strategic partnership. Per the Globe, the deal will deepen co-operation in defence, energy and joint ventures with the country of 87 million, and it marks the first-ever official bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey. This is part of a broader pattern, with Ottawa framing the trip as reducing reliance on the increasingly protectionist and unpredictable United States under Donald Trump. While there, Carney addressed accusations of Canadian meddling in the US midterms, saying there's no merit to the claims and that he's disappointed the American envoy keeps repeating them.

That midterm story has a second layer at home. CBC reports Canadian diplomats based in the US have been told to avoid appearing with midterm candidates, and Industry Minister Joly separately pushed back on meddling accusations, saying she'd never interfere because she expects the same from Washington.

Closer to home, CBC confirms a deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright started on an automatic grenade launcher range, despite earlier orders to close gas wells on the base. Investigators are still piecing together how the blaze spread.

blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Industry structure, lesson 6: Retail and consumer: unit economics and same store sales.

Start with the number every retail analyst quotes first: same store sales, also called comparable sales or comps. It measures revenue growth only from stores open at least a year, stripping out new openings. That matters because a retailer can grow total revenue nicely while every existing store is actually losing ground, just by opening new boxes. Comps tell you whether the core business is getting healthier, not just bigger.

Take Dollarama's fiscal 2024 results, reported in the company's fourth quarter release in April 2024. Total revenue grew roughly 9% for the year. Comparable store sales grew 4.6%. Break that 4.6% into its two drivers: transaction count and average basket size. The growth came mostly from basket size, meaning customers spent more per visit, not that more customers walked in. That is a pricing and mix story, the same pricing power signal you learned to spot in filings two lessons back, now showing up at the register.

The one mistake people make is stopping at the headline revenue number and assuming it reflects store level health. A chain can post double digit revenue growth purely from store count expansion while comps sit flat or negative. That means existing locations are stagnant, and the growth is really a capital deployment story, not a demand story. Always ask which number you are looking at before you draw a conclusion.

Your task today, under fifteen minutes. Open Thomson ONE, pull one consumer retailer's segment data or management discussion and analysis. Find comparable sales growth for the last two reported quarters, compare it to total revenue growth for the same periods, and write down the gap in percentage points, noting whether it is widening or narrowing.

Here is what comps actually prove and what they cannot. They prove whether existing operations are gaining or losing ground with customers, and they hint at pricing versus volume. They cannot tell you store level margins, return on invested capital, or whether that growth is even profitable. That is why comps come after your analysis step and feed into company against sector, never replace the work itself.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 19: Individual pension plans for incorporated professionals.

An individual pension plan, or IPP, is a defined benefit pension plan built for one person, usually the owner of an incorporated professional corporation. It only works with T4 salary income, not dividends. That's the detail people miss after years of taking dividends for tax efficiency.

Here's why it matters. For 2026, the RRSP dollar limit is 33,810 dollars, up from 32,490 in 2025, per the Canada Revenue Agency's indexed figures. An IPP contribution room formula is age based and actuarial, so past age 50 it regularly beats the RRSP limit by a wide margin.

Worked example. Dr. Singh, 58 years old, incorporated, has paid herself T4 salary of 200,000 dollars a year for the past decade. Her IPP actuary calculates a required contribution of roughly 62,000 dollars for this year alone, almost double the 2026 RRSP limit. Because her corporation existed and paid her T4 income back to age 48, she can also fund past service, a one time catch up contribution that in her case runs close to 180,000 dollars, fully tax deductible to the corporation. That's money moved out of corporate retained earnings into a creditor protected, tax sheltered pension, all deductible against active business income.

The one mistake: assuming an IPP works for a dividend only shareholder. It doesn't. CRA requires pensionable T4 earnings to calculate the benefit, so if you've optimized your comp mix toward dividends for payroll tax savings, you've accidentally disqualified yourself from the IPP's biggest advantage.

In Manitoba, an IPP sponsored by a Manitoba employer falls under the Manitoba Pension Benefits Act. Funds are locked in, same as any registered pension, and at retirement they convert to a Manitoba locked in retirement account and eventually a prescribed registered retirement income fund, not a regular RRIF. Less withdrawal flexibility than an RRSP, more certainty of funding.

Communication, lesson 19: Feedback: giving it so it lands and receiving it without defending.

Kim Scott ran ad sales at Google before she coached Sheryl Sandberg at Facebook. She gave a polished presentation once, confident, well-rehearsed. Afterward Sandberg said, "That was great, but you said um a lot." Scott brushed it off. Weeks later Sandberg stopped her cold: "When you say um every third word, it makes you sound stupid." That version landed. Scott fixed it within a month. She built Radical Candor from that moment: care personally, challenge directly, together, never instead of each other.

The model that makes this teachable comes from the Center for Creative Leadership: Situation, Behavior, Impact. Name the situation, describe the observable behavior, state the impact. Nothing about character.

Worked example. Not: "You're disorganized." Instead: "In yesterday's board call, you ran seven minutes over your update, and two directors left before the vote." Situation: yesterday's call. Behavior: seven minutes over. Impact: two directors missed the vote. Specific enough to act on, far enough from identity that the brain doesn't treat it as a threat.

Gallup's 2023 State of the Global Workplace found only 23 percent of employees strongly agree that feedback they receive actually helps them improve. Most feedback fails not because it's unkind, because it's vague.

Here's the one mistake, and it shows up on the receiving end. Someone says, "you cut me off in that meeting," and you answer, "I was just trying to add something," before you've asked a single question. Douglas Stone and Sheila Heen, who wrote Thanks for the Feedback out of the Harvard Negotiation Project, call this the switchtrack. You hear a judgment and respond to a different conversation entirely, the one about whether you're a bad person, instead of the one about the behavior.

Today's task takes under fifteen minutes. Before you give feedback to anyone this week, write one sentence using Situation, Behavior, Impact, nothing else.

blocks.title: PHP Flaw, Hormuz Fears, Meta's Big AI Bet
blocks.script: Good evening. Here is a look at the stories and companies dominating business news over the past two days, drawn from the Globe and Mail's Report on Business. The biggest alarm is a serious flaw in the PHP programming language, uncovered with the help of AI tools. Developers rushed out fixes Wednesday, but the bug had sat hidden for years, and companies and governments worldwide are now fending off millions of hacking attempts while they patch. The tailwind is that fixes exist and are spreading fast. The headwind is that so much infrastructure runs on PHP that full cleanup will take time. An evidence-based advisor would call this an operational risk to monitor, not a reason to dump cybersecurity names. Geopolitical risk flared again as Iran said seven oil tankers were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran hinting it could widen any conflict to undersea cables and data centres. That raises fears of broader war and could unsettle energy and shipping markets. Tesla surprised investors with positive free cash flow and lower than expected AI spending, even as its core car business faces pressure from cheaper global rivals. The discipline is a tailwind, but intensifying EV competition remains a headwind. Advisors would say the cash flow beat is encouraging but shouldn't override a long term valuation view. Meta had an eventful stretch. It is putting its Muse AI agent at the centre of its strategy and plans a new class of stock to fund investments without diluting Mark Zuckerberg's control, sending shares higher after hours. At the same time, Meta was hit with a twenty five billion dollar penalty in New Mexico over misleading users in the Cambridge Analytica case. AI ambition is a clear tailwind; mounting legal costs are a real headwind, not noise. IBM raised its annual software revenue outlook to roughly seven to eight percent growth, a sign of steady execution in enterprise software and AI tools.
talkingPoints: The PHP vulnerability is a reminder that cybersecurity exposure can touch almost any portfolio holding enterprise software.
Strait of Hormuz tensions could quickly feed into energy prices and shipping costs.
Tesla and Meta show spending discipline now matters as much as AI ambition to investors.
Canadian defence and space funding is growing, but access to capital for smaller firms remains a gap.

blocks.title: Succession Gaps, Cyber Risks, and ETF Records Lead Advisor News
blocks.script: Good morning. Here is what Canadian wealth advisors need to know today. New research from Wells Fargo, reported by Wealth Professional, finds that conflict over inheritance is now the norm rather than the exception. The study points to a wide gap between how affluent parents and their adult children understand and prepare for passing on family wealth, a reminder for advisors to get succession conversations started early and often. On the business side, a Canadian Federation of Independent Business report cited by Wealth Professional warns that two trillion dollars in small business value is at risk because most owners lack a formal exit plan. That is a major opening for advisors working with incorporated business owners who may not have started succession planning at all. Cybersecurity is also front of mind. Wealth Professional reports that a global programming flaw, combined with a new national survey, is forcing Canadian advisors to confront the real cost of a data breach to client trust. Separately, a related website vulnerability has already taken down European government sites and affected major platforms like Wikipedia, and advisor websites are not immune. On the regulatory front, the Financial Stability Board has pitched eight principles to modernize financial rules, and Canada's OSFI reforms made the list. The industry has until January to respond. Meanwhile, CIRO has issued hearing notices for Goldman Sachs Canada and advisor Graeme Hamilton, the latter facing allegations tied to discretionary trading and due diligence. And a cautionary tale for compliance teams: an investor who flagged possible fraud in a land banking group back in 2018 saw her lawsuit tossed because it was filed more than three years later, missing the limitation deadline. On product trends, ETF assets in Canada hit a sixth straight monthly record, with 17.7 billion dollars in inflows in September, according to Wealth Professional, even as mutual funds posted their first net redemptions in 16 months. A new SPIVA Canada Scorecard also shows even top-quartile Canadian funds lagged their benchmarks in the first half of 2026. And a new cross-border firm, Sonance Financial, has launched with 2.3 billion dollars in combined assets from four partners, backed by Miami-based Trivest Partners. For clients, CLHIA data shows Canadian life and health insurers paid out 157 billion dollars in benefits last year, up 10 per cent, while managing more than 680 billion in retirement assets. The Globe and Mail also flags year-end tax strategies for seniors, including watching the OAS clawback line and splitting pension income with a spouse.

blocks.title: Tax Hikes, Tory Walkout, and a Downtown Crane Falls
blocks.script: The big Winnipeg story tonight is Wednesday's mayoral debate on CBC, one week before voting day. Kevin Klein didn't need to win it, he needed to knock Mike Vogiatzakis out as the real alternative to incumbent Scott Gillingham, and by CBC's own read, he managed that over the supper hour after stumbling earlier on CJOB radio. The number that matters for you: all three front runners, Gillingham, Klein and Vogiatzakis, said yes when asked if they'd raise property taxes. Gillingham is locked into the 3.5 per cent hike already built into the city's four year budget. Vogiatzakis wants a freeze through 2027 and likely 2028 before any increase. Klein says taxes rise to pay for 100 more police officers, with his full costed number due Friday. Whoever wins, build a Winnipeg property tax increase into client cash flow for next year. At the Legislature, the Progressive Conservatives are defending a decision to cut the fall sitting short by a week, four days gone, saying the NDP government had nothing left worth staying for. Downtown, the tower crane has come down at the old Bay building. That's a three hundred ten million dollar Southern Chiefs' Organization redevelopment, about two years from completion, and a real signal for downtown Winnipeg real estate confidence. In the southeast, late season rain turned into a bumper soybean crop for some growers after a shift away from wheat, CBC reports. Riley Laychuk's forecast has southern Manitoba near twenty degrees today, with snow possible up north by the weekend. In court, Manitoba's Court of Appeal is hearing that the province's 2024 moose licence cut was unlawful, about two hundred hunters affected, brought by Pimicikamak and a conservation group. In the Interlake, minor hockey loses its under fifteen and under eighteen co-ed divisions again, those teams cleared to play in Winnipeg instead. RCMP seized two hundred seventy nine thousand dollars in drugs at a northern Manitoba airport.

blocks.title: Carney Unveils Aid Package, Faces Bill Pushback
blocks.script: Good evening. Several federal stories are developing today involving Prime Minister Mark Carney's government, from new industry spending to criticism over proposed legislation. Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced a multibillion dollar support package for sectors hit by US tariffs. CBC reports the partnership totals eight point seven billion dollars, covering steel, auto and critical minerals, along with funding for a road into Ontario's Ring of Fire mining region. In prepared remarks, Carney said US tariffs have put Ontario workers and businesses, in his words, "at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty." Separately, more than fifty fellows of the Royal Society of Canada are warning Ottawa that fast-tracking major projects under Bill C-39 risks causing irreversible environmental harm. The scientists are urging the government to reconsider provisions they say would weaken environmental protections. On trade, the Globe and Mail reports Canada and the European Union plan to firm up a new "alliance for the future" at a Montreal summit next week. A draft joint statement obtained by the paper says Canada would be treated as an associate member of the twenty-seven country bloc, with cooperation on trade, defence and other ties. Meanwhile, the government's lawful-access bill, known as Bill C-22, is drawing more corporate pushback. Swiss privacy company Proton says expansion into Canada would become impossible if the bill passes in its current form, joining other firms including Signal and Windscribe that have warned the legislation could weaken encryption and threaten user privacy. A new analysis found French content in Carney's public speeches has risen from seventeen to twenty-three per cent, according to CBC.

blocks.title: PHP Flaw, Agentic Shopping Split, and AI Debt Doubts
blocks.script: The biggest technology story today is a global cybersecurity scramble around PHP, the programming language that runs something like seventy percent of websites worldwide, per CNN's reporting. OpenAI and Google's Wiz both say they used artificial intelligence, including OpenAI's GPT-5.6 and Google's Gemini models, to uncover two critical flaws that sat hidden in the PHP code for more than a decade. Wiz compared it to Heartbleed, the 2014 bug that rattled the internet. Canada's Centre for Cyber Security issued an urgent alert this week, and government websites here, including Statistics Canada, went briefly offline while agencies rushed to patch, the Globe and Mail reports. For your clients, this is the sharp edge of AI in security. The same tools that found the hole also make it faster for someone else to exploit it now that the flaw is public. If a client runs a business website on PHP or WordPress, this is the week to ask whether their provider has patched it. On the corporate AI front, Walmart and Amazon just split in opposite directions, TechCrunch reports. Amazon is blocking AI shopping agents from buying on its site. Walmart launched an Agent Gateway that lets approved AI agents purchase on a customer's behalf, with spending limits and approval controls. It is an early test of how retail competes once software, not people, does the clicking, and it matters for any client with exposure to either company. On financing, Blackstone's AI infrastructure head, Jas Khaira, told TechCrunch fears over AI buildout debt are overblown, worth flagging given how much leveraged financing is flowing into data centers right now.

blocks.title: Four Minutes, Mars Hearts, and Gambling Ads
blocks.script:
A new Penn State trial, published in PLOS One, finds four minutes of daily strength exercise meaningfully improves balance, leg strength, and the ability to stand up from a chair in adults over 65. Ninety seven sedentary participants, average age 74, were randomly split into an exercise group and a control group doing four 30 second moves: push-ups, chair stands, band rows, and stair stepping. After 12 weeks, the exercise group gained more than four extra chair stands and nearly three and a half seconds of single leg balance versus control. It's a trial under 100 people, but it strengthens the case that brief resistance work cuts fall risk.

A separate study in Circulation tracked 13 astronauts through six month missions on the space station. Heart function dipped early in weightlessness, then recovered, and after landing none showed more cardiovascular strain under simulated Mars gravity than before flight. The protective factor was up to two hours of daily cardio and resistance training. Thirteen people is a small sample, but it's a strong signal for how much exercise buffers the body under extreme stress.

blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Terminal value: where most DCFs go wrong
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Valuation reps, lesson 5: Terminal value: where most DCFs go wrong.

Here is the number that should bother you every time you build a discounted cash flow, DCF. In a typical five-year model, terminal value often makes up seventy to eighty percent of the total valuation. You spend four weeks modeling revenue growth, margins, and working capital for years one through five, and then one formula, covering everything from year six to infinity, carries most of the weight.

The two methods are the Gordon growth model and the exit multiple. Gordon growth takes your final year free cash flow, grows it by a perpetual rate, usually two to three percent, matching long run gross domestic product, GDP, and divides by the discount rate minus that growth rate. Say your year five free cash flow is 100 million dollars, your discount rate, your weighted average cost of capital, WACC, is nine percent, and perpetual growth is two and a half percent. Terminal value equals 100 million times 1.025, divided by, 0.09 minus 0.025. That is 102.5 million divided by 0.065, which equals roughly 1.58 billion dollars. Discount that back five years at nine percent and you still get around 1.03 billion dollars, dwarfing the four years of explicit cash flow before it.

The one mistake: people pick a growth rate close to the discount rate. Move that perpetual growth from two and a half to three and a half percent, and terminal value jumps to 1.82 billion, a seventeen percent swing from one input nobody stress tested. The formula is mathematically sensitive near that gap, and that sensitivity is exactly where optimism hides.

What this reveals: your valuation is really a bet on one number, the spread between WACC and perpetual growth. What it cannot tell you: whether that spread is even knowable ten years out. This is why you look at analysis first, then technicals, then company against sector, because the DCF output means nothing without that context.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Mega-mergers, power deals and steel jobs collide
blocks.script: Good evening. Tonight we track the ten companies drawing the most attention across business and markets, with a Canadian lens on energy, autos and steel. Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. Paramount is the US media company now controlled through Skydance; Warner Bros is the studio behind HBO and CNN. Paramount has closed its roughly 110 billion dollar takeover, creating a new Hollywood giant. Tailwind: scale across film, streaming and news. Headwind: regulators and consumers worry about concentration and higher prices. An evidence-based advisor would say don't chase media consolidation, synergy promises rarely translate cleanly into returns. Google and Constellation Energy. Google is Alphabet's cloud and search arm; Constellation is a major US power and nuclear generator. The two struck a 3.6 gigawatt power deal, with Constellation committing over 4.3 billion dollars in new fleet investment. Tailwind: AI-driven power demand. Headwind: execution and regulatory timelines. Advisors say power-for-AI deals are a durable theme, but valuations already price in plenty of optimism. ATCO and Canadian Utilities, with Nova Scotia's Emera. ATCO is proposing a roughly 35 billion dollar merger of Canadian Utilities with Emera, part of what's being called a 72 billion dollar utility bet. ATCO's Nancy Southern calls it a win-win, creating the pure-play utility analysts favour. Tailwind: scale and simpler structure. Headwind: integration and cross-border approvals. An advisor would call this classic defensive consolidation, fine for income, not growth. CPPIB, AT&T and BlackRock's GIP. Canada's pension giant is joining AT&T and BlackRock's infrastructure arm in a fibre-optic venture funding broadband across 16 US states. Tailwind: steady infrastructure cash flows. Headwind: capital intensity and slow payback. Advisors see textbook pension infrastructure investing, hard for retail investors to replicate. Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs. Stelco is the Hamilton steelmaker owned by US-based Cleveland-Cliffs. Ottawa has given the owner five business days to produce a jobs plan or face possible legal action, while Stelco's exit from galvanized steel has left buyer Cascadia Metals, fresh off a 30 million dollar plant expansion for domestic steel, scrambling. Tailwind: federal pressure could protect jobs. Headwind: trade uncertainty keeps squeezing Canadian steel. Advisors call this a politically exposed, volatile sector. GM in Oshawa and Stellantis in Brampton. GM will end light-duty Silverado production in Oshawa while boosting heavy-duty output, saying jobs should hold. Stellantis workers will vote on strike action after Unifor walked from talks once the automaker confirmed selling its Brampton plant to a defence contractor. Tailwind: heavy-duty demand. Headwind: labour unrest. Advisors treat auto names as cyclical and sensitive to labour headlines. Bombardier.
talkingPoints: Mega-mergers in media and utilities are concentrating power in fewer hands, from Skydance-Warner to ATCO-Emera.
AI-driven power demand, seen in Google's Constellation deal, is reshaping utility investment.
Canadian steel and auto jobs remain politically fraught, with Ottawa pressing Stelco's owner and Stellantis workers readying a strike vote.

blocks.title: Baby Costs, Hospital Beds, and Language Politics in Manitoba
blocks.script: The biggest Manitoba story today is the squeeze on young families. CBC Manitoba reports prices for baby formula and diapers are climbing in Winnipeg just as donations to assistance programs are dropping, pushing some parents into what advocates call heartbreaking situations, with at least one local program now having to cover more of those costs itself. If you sit on a board for a family or children's charity, that funding gap is worth raising this quarter. On health care, the province says it's adding more than 100 community-based care spaces in Winnipeg for patients who are medically cleared but have nowhere to go, the goal being to free up hospital beds and cut emergency room wait times. It's part of a broader expansion of post-hospital support for homeless and mental health patients. At the Legislature, Premier Wab Kinew has been answering English questions in French for two straight days in question period. A political scientist interviewed by CBC called it an unhealthy politicizing of language, adding friction to a sitting that's already unsettled after a Tory caucus departure last week. On addictions policy, the minister responsible for housing and homelessness says Winnipeg's supervised consumption site is making its surrounding neighbourhood even safer than before, though CBC notes not every nearby resident agrees. On regulation, new provincial legislation would let cannabis retailers remove the window coverings they're currently required to keep up, a safety response after assaults on store staff. Separately, a Manitoba pharmacy owner who reported her own business partner for misusing narcotics has herself been fined fifteen thousand dollars for inadequate oversight of controlled substances, a case worth flagging if you advise anyone in pharmacy or health-sector ownership. On crime, Winnipeg police seized 26 kilograms of cocaine and about $750,000 in cash in a south Winnipeg raid. The RCMP laid 21 new charges in the Bunibonibee drug-trafficking investigation up north. In Osborne Village, a man and woman face charges after assaults that sent two people to hospital. And a U.S. appeals court upheld the conviction in the human smuggling case tied to the 2022 deaths of an Indian family at the Manitoba border near Emerson. Briefly: Uber has permanently banned a driver after an alleged sexual assault in Winnipeg's Weston neighbourhood. Brandon University researchers are sampling frogs and salamanders across the province, expecting to confirm the chytrid fungus, a pathogen with reported presence everywhere around Manitoba, already blamed for the extinction of at least 90 amphibian species worldwide.

blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Holding companies: when they help and when they add cost / Difficult conversations: separating the person from the problem
blocks.script:
Financial Planning Facts, lesson 18: Holding companies: when they help and when they add cost.

A holding company, or Holdco, is just a corporation that owns shares in your operating company, Opco, instead of holding your business assets directly. The dividend from Opco to Holdco moves tax-free under section 112 of the Income Tax Act, because it's an inter-corporate dividend between connected corporations. That's the whole trick. You're not avoiding tax, you're deferring and protecting.

Here's where it helps. Say your Opco in Manitoba has $300,000 of retained earnings sitting as cash, earning interest inside the company. Manitoba's small business rate is 0% federally reduced, so combined with the federal small business rate your Opco pays roughly 9% on the first $500,000 of active income in 2026. But if that $300,000 cash sits in Opco, it's exposed to business creditors, and it pushes up passive investment income, which for 2026 still grinds your $500,000 small business limit dollar for dollar once passive income passes $50,000, fully gone at $150,000. Move that $300,000 to Holdco as a tax-free dividend, and Opco's balance sheet is cleaner for lenders, creditors can't reach it, and you've separated the investment pool from the operating risk.

Where it costs you: a second corporation means a second set of financial statements, a second tax return, separate minute books, and typically another $2,500 to $5,000 a year in accounting and legal fees in Manitoba. If your retained earnings are under roughly $150,000, that cost often outweighs the benefit.

The mistake I see constantly: business owners strip cash into a Holdco after they're already being sued or after a creditor claim exists. That's a fraudulent conveyance, courts will unwind it, and CRA plus creditors both go looking. The protection only works if you move the cash before the liability exists, as routine planning, not as a reaction.

Communication, lesson 18: Difficult conversations: separating the person from the problem.

Picture this. You're on a nonprofit board, and the treasurer wants to cut the youth program budget from 40,000 dollars to 28,000 dollars to cover a shortfall. You think he's being reckless. He thinks you're being sentimental. Within ten minutes, it's not about the number anymore. It's about who's right and who's careless with other people's money.

Roger Fisher and William Ury at the Harvard Negotiation Project named this problem in Getting to Yes, back in 1981: people fuse the issue with the identity of the person raising it. Their fix is one sentence: separate the people from the problem. You treat the person as someone you're working alongside, and you put the problem on the table in front of both of you, not between you.

Here's how that plays out with the 12,000 dollar gap. Instead of saying "you're gutting the program," you say, "we have a 12,000 dollar gap, and I want to find it without cutting the mentoring hours. What are you protecting when you propose this cut, and what am I protecting when I resist it?" Now you're both looking at the same number, with two different interests on the table: his interest is solvency, yours is program continuity. That's a problem you can solve together.
