lessons.label: Financial Planning Facts
lessons.title: Holding companies: when they help and when they add cost
lessons.script:
A holding company, or Holdco, is just a corporation that owns shares in your operating company, Opco, instead of holding your business assets directly. The dividend from Opco to Holdco moves tax-free under section 112 of the Income Tax Act, because it's an inter-corporate dividend between connected corporations. That's the whole trick. You're not avoiding tax, you're deferring and protecting.

Here's where it helps. Say your Opco in Manitoba has $300,000 of retained earnings sitting as cash, earning interest inside the company. Manitoba's small business rate is 0% federally reduced, so combined with the federal small business rate your Opco pays roughly 9% on the first $500,000 of active income in 2026. But if that $300,000 cash sits in Opco, it's exposed to business creditors, and it pushes up passive investment income, which for 2026 still grinds your $500,000 small business limit dollar for dollar once passive income passes $50,000, fully gone at $150,000. Move that $300,000 to Holdco as a tax-free dividend, and Opco's balance sheet is cleaner for lenders, creditors can't reach it, and you've separated the investment pool from the operating risk.

Where it costs you: a second corporation means a second set of financial statements, a second tax return, separate minute books, and typically another $2,500 to $5,000 a year in accounting and legal fees in Manitoba. If your retained earnings are under roughly $150,000, that cost often outweighs the benefit.

The mistake I see constantly: business owners strip cash into a Holdco after they're already being sued or after a creditor claim exists. That's a fraudulent conveyance, courts will unwind it, and CRA plus creditors both go looking. The protection only works if you move the cash before the liability exists, as routine planning, not as a reaction.

lessons.label: Communication
lessons.title: Difficult conversations: separating the person from the problem
lessons.script:
Picture this. You're on a nonprofit board, and the treasurer wants to cut the youth program budget from 40,000 dollars to 28,000 dollars to cover a shortfall. You think he's being reckless. He thinks you're being sentimental. Within ten minutes, it's not about the number anymore. It's about who's right and who's careless with other people's money.

Roger Fisher and William Ury at the Harvard Negotiation Project named this problem in Getting to Yes, back in 1981: people fuse the issue with the identity of the person raising it. Their fix is one sentence: separate the people from the problem. You treat the person as someone you're working alongside, and you put the problem on the table in front of both of you, not between you.

Here's how that plays out with the 12,000 dollar gap. Instead of saying "you're gutting the program," you say, "we have a 12,000 dollar gap, and I want to find it without cutting the mentoring hours. What are you protecting when you propose this cut, and what am I protecting when I resist it?" Now you're both looking at the same number, with two different interests on the table: his interest is solvency, yours is program continuity. That's a problem you can solve together. Maybe you find 8,000 dollars in deferred vendor payments and split the remaining 4,000 across two fiscal quarters.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Bond Contagion Fears Rattle Europe, Loonie Slides
blocks.script:
Start with what is rattling global bond markets right now, because it will come up with clients today. French, Italian, Belgian and Greek government bonds, which normally move together, broke apart on Thursday and sold off hard at the same time. Bloomberg reports a Morgan Stanley portfolio manager says traders are seeing the first signs of contagion, the word everyone remembers from Europe's debt crisis fifteen years ago. The euro fell to its weakest level in seventeen months against the US dollar on the back of it. That dollar strength spilled into Canada too. The Globe and Mail reports the loonie touched an eighteen month low, with speculators raising bearish bets, even as it traded close to 70 US cents.

None of that stopped Canadian and US equities. The TSX closed up nearly one percent, just above 35,500. The S&P 500 added about three quarters of a percent, the Nasdaq better than one percent. That follows Friday's softer US jobs data, which pared back bets on another Federal Reserve hike this month, with traders now pricing less than a one in four chance.

On the Bank of Canada, the overnight rate has been held at 2.25 percent since September 2, the seventh straight hold. The next announcement is October 28, with a full Monetary Policy Report attached. That one matters, because inflation is stuck near three percent and oil prices are elevated, so markets are genuinely split between another hold and a surprise hike.

On jobs, Statistics Canada's most recent report showed the economy lost 42,000 positions in August, ending a hot four month run of hiring, while the unemployment rate held at 6.4 percent.

In energy, oil slipped again toward 90 dollars US, as the G7 taps emergency reserves to calm supply nerves. Calgary's Suncor is selling its stakes in three Newfoundland offshore fields to Ithaca Energy for 1.2 billion dollars. Gold is holding just above 4,160 dollars an ounce, still near record highs.
talkingPoints: Watch the Bank of Canada's October 28 decision, a hike is back on the table, not just a hold.
Euro zone bond stress is a real risk to watch, it already pushed our dollar to an eighteen month low.
TSX and Wall Street keep grinding higher even with the bond noise, don't let clients overreact.
August's jobs loss shows the labour market cooling, worth flagging for anyone nervous about their own position.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Utility Mega-Deal Leads Busy Week For Dealmakers
blocks.script: Good evening. Tonight we're tracking the companies drawing the most attention over the past two days, led by a wave of mergers and takeover activity across Canada's utility, energy and cannabis sectors. Emera and Canadian Utilities: Emera is the Halifax-based utility behind Nova Scotia Power, with operations across North America and the Caribbean. It has made a friendly all-stock bid for Canadian Utilities, the Alberta company at the heart of the ATCO group, in a deal the Globe and Mail values near 35 billion dollars. The tailwind is scale, since the merger would create one of the 20 largest utilities in North America. The headwind is the complexity of winning regulatory approval across multiple jurisdictions. An evidence-based advisor would tell clients utility mergers this size take months to clear, so patience matters more than chasing the stock now. Cenovus and Athabasca Oil: Cenovus is one of Canada's largest integrated oil producers, and it has agreed to buy oilsands player Athabasca Oil as part of a growth push. The Globe notes the deal has analysts scouting a new generation of oil patch takeover targets. The tailwind is consolidation appetite in the oilsands; the headwind is ongoing commodity price volatility. An advisor would caution against chasing takeover rumours in small-cap energy names, since that is speculation, not investing. Curaleaf and Aurora Cannabis: Curaleaf is a major US cannabis operator that has sweetened its offer for Toronto-based Aurora Cannabis, now targeting roughly five US dollars a share. The tailwind is sector consolidation finally offering shareholders an exit; the headwind is Aurora's long record of value destruction since legalization. An advisor would frame this as a one-time event to evaluate, not a long-term cannabis thesis. Cohere: The Toronto AI company unveiled a new version of its North platform with more agentic features, aimed at winning corporate and government customers. The tailwind is strong enterprise AI demand; the headwind is intense competition from much larger global rivals. An advisor would note Cohere is still private, so there is no direct public market way in yet. Nutrien: The Saskatchewan fertilizer giant is indefinitely shutting its Trinidad nitrogen operations due to natural gas supply constraints. That's a near-term headwind for volumes, though global fertilizer demand remains a longer-term tailwind. An advisor would call this a contained operational issue rather than a reason to rethink the stock.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Election Discontent, Tesla's Court Fight, Hydro's Big Loss
blocks.script: Start with the municipal election, because it's the conversation every client is having right now. A new Abacus Data poll, commissioned by the Free Press, finds half of Winnipeggers think the city is heading in the wrong direction, with only twenty one percent saying it's on the right track. Four in ten say they get poor value for their property tax dollars. That discontent is shaping the mayoral race: challenger Kevin Klein is pledging to restore the city ombudsman position, cut more than two decades ago, while incumbent Scott Gillingham has leaned softer, proposing a park along the Seine River. Out in Waverley West, the city's biggest and fastest growing ward, five candidates are running on how to manage that growth, and province wide, the Association of Manitoba Municipalities says acclamations are down this year, meaning more communities actually have a choice on the ballot. Advance voting opened Monday. On the Tesla file, now in court. Tesla's lawyers argued in front of a Manitoba Court of King's Bench judge that the province's decision to cut the company from the EV rebate program was politically motivated and unfair, pointing to Premier Wab Kinew's own past comments tying the exclusion to Elon Musk's politics. The province counters that it was a budget decision and not reviewable by the courts. That rebate was worth up to four thousand dollars a vehicle. Manitoba Hydro is on the watch list, and it had a rough year. The Crown corporation's annual report shows a four hundred forty six million dollar loss for twenty twenty five, twenty six, driven by drought that forced Hydro to import almost as much power as it exported. The energy regulator is still weighing a plan to free up over a quarter of Hydro's generating capacity, including a three billion dollar gas plant expansion in Brandon. Two government bills landed this week. One lets cannabis stores remove window coverings, after reports of assaults on staff. The other strengthens protections for survivors of intimate partner violence. In Morden, the family of a young woman who died after a dental procedure is suing the dentist and clinic over a local anesthetic injected into a blood vessel. On crime and courts: Manitoba's Court of Appeal ruled the People's Party of Canada partly liable in a Winnipeg defamation case. RCMP seized thirteen guns and twenty thousand rounds of ammunition from two homes in West St. Paul.

blocks.title: Ottawa Reshapes Defence Buying, Security Probes Widen
blocks.script:
Good evening. We start in Ottawa, where sources tell the Globe and Mail the federal government plans to turn its year-old Defence Investment Agency into a Crown corporation. CBC reports the move is meant to break a long-standing logjam in Canada's defence procurement system. The change would hand chief executive Doug Guzman far more authority over purchasing decisions, though it raises questions about oversight and accountability that officials have yet to fully answer.

Security concerns are also in focus after Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said Canadian law enforcement may get involved in the case of an alleged NATO spy once a Belgian inquiry concludes. Anandasangaree told CBC the case points to gaps in Canada's security screening that need addressing, with Canadian departments now facing scrutiny over the person's activities here.

The Department of National Defence confirmed two members of the Canadian Armed Forces were arrested by Toronto police as part of a probe into organized crime, kidnapping and firearms theft. DND says it is cooperating with the investigation.

In Alberta, MPs are reacting to a Globe and Mail investigation showing separatist leaders met with Republican political operatives and offered access to provincial resources, including fresh water, forestry and mining, in exchange for American support. Calgary Liberal MP Corey Hogan said Canada may need to review laws around this kind of freelance diplomacy, though he stopped short of calling it treasonous.

And on the world stage, mapmakers are grappling with a presidential edict from Donald Trump over naming conventions on Lake Ontario, with a United Nations group meeting this month to look at bringing order to how such disputes are handled globally.

blocks.label: Health & Fitness
blocks.title: Fasting Study Shows Day-Three Turning Point
blocks.script: The biggest health story today is about fasting, and it matters if you train. Scientists at Queen Mary University of London monitored 12 healthy volunteers during a seven day water-only fast, tracking roughly 3,000 proteins circulating in the bloodstream. The body quickly shifted from burning glucose to burning fat within the first two to three days of fasting, but the most notable biological changes only appeared after about three days without calories. The findings are published in Nature Metabolism, but with only twelve people, call it early stage, not a prescription. One flag if you lift: participants lost an average of 5.7 kilograms, including both fat and lean tissue, and while most of the lean tissue loss returned once eating resumed, you are down real muscle during the fast itself.
talkingPoints: A seven day water only fast shows its biggest molecular shifts after day three, not right away.

blocks.script: The biggest development story this week: new research reported by ScienceDaily found that stimulating the vagus nerve right after a mouse practices a new motor skill helped that skill stick for good, more than practice alone. The effect tracked with rhythmic changes in brain blood vessels, suggesting the body sends signals that help the brain lock in new learning. It is mice, not toddlers, but it strengthens the case that timing and rest after practice matter for how skills become permanent. blocks.script: Good evening. We start in the NHL, where the Winnipeg Jets picked up a road win. The unbeaten Ottawa Senators rolled past Boston 4-1, with Tim Stutzle posting three points and moving into sole possession of sixth on Ottawa's all-time scoring list. In Vegas, Marc Gatcomb's go-ahead goal, plus a Mitch Marner tally, lifted the Golden Knights past Vancouver 3-2. And in Toronto, coach Craig Hiller is patiently waiting on his Tavares-Nylander-McKenna line, which has combined for just five points through three games. The biggest hockey headline came from Washington, where captain Alex Ovechkin announced his 22nd NHL season will be his last. The league's all-time goals leader will play nine games in Canada this season, including a November 10th stop in Ottawa, his first game north of the border since April. Elsewhere, Canadian soccer internationals Cyle Larin and Tajon Buchanan both left the men's national team with injuries.
